content.text: Sister's 30th Birthday Party

A memorable, personal celebration that feels like her: relaxed, fun, and full of the people she loves. Write the one-sentence vibe here and keep every decision tied to it.

Surprise or not? Decide and tell co-organizers
Pick the date and a backup date
Choose venue (home, restaurant, rented space, outdoors)
Lock in the theme and dress code
Set total budget and who is chipping in
Theme & style
Theme: e.g. 'Dirty Thirty', garden party, 2000s throwback
Colour palette: pick 2-3 colours
Signature drink and cake flavour she loves
Special touches
Ideas: photo wall of her 30 years, a video of messages from friends and family, a toast or speech, a playlist of songs from each decade of her life.

suggestions.title: Interview prep plan
suggestions.reason: A day-by-day plan for the week so nothing is left to the last minute

content.text: Interview Prep Plan
Goal: walk in confident, knowing the company, the role, and my 5-6 strongest stories cold.
This week
Day 1: Re-read the job description and highlight the top 5 requirements
Day 2: Finish company research (product, customers, competitors, recent news)
Day 3: Write STAR stories and map each to a competency
Day 4: Review fintech domain topics and technical or case material
Day 5: Mock interview out loud, timed, with a friend or recording
Day 6: Light review, prepare questions to ask, plan outfit and logistics
Day before
Confirm time, location or video link, and interviewer names
Print or open resume copies and my notes
Test camera, mic, and internet if remote
Get to bed early
Day of
Skim my pitch and top 3 stories, do a 5-minute warm-up out loud, arrive or log in 10 minutes early, and send thank-you notes within 24 hours.

Payments and money movement

Chargebacks, disputes, and fraud liability
Risk, compliance, and security
KYC, AML, and sanctions screening basics
PCI DSS, SOC 2, and data privacy (GDPR, CCPA)
Fraud detection approaches and the false-positive tradeoff
Platform and engineering concepts
Double-entry ledgers and reconciliation

Business metrics

content.text: Launch content campaign: 6-week brief
Goal

Build awareness and a qualified pipeline ahead of the 14 November 2026 launch, then convert that attention into demo requests and signups in launch week. Replace the targets below with your real numbers.

Economic buyer: the budget holder (VP or founder) who needs a clear ROI story
Influencers: the practitioners and partners they trust
Key messages
The problem: what is broken today, and what it costs
The shift: how the product changes the workflow
The proof: demo video, early customer quotes, numbers
Six-week plan
Week 1 (5 Oct): Foundations. Messaging locked, tracking set up, content calendar filled.
Week 2 (12 Oct): Problem awareness. Thought-leadership posts and the first blog pieces.
Week 3 (19 Oct): Education. Webinar promotion, how-to content and podcast appearances.
Week 4 (26 Oct): Proof. Demo video, customer stories, a waitlist or early-access push.
Week 5 (2 Nov): Pre-launch. Press release, teaser emails, paid retargeting.
Week 6 (9 Nov): Launch. Announcement across all channels on 14 Nov, then follow-up.
Team roles (proposed)
Sam: written content, press and podcast outreach
Priya: launch lead, video and campaign messaging
Alex: paid channels, tracking, analytics and billing readiness

content.text: Monthly landlord routine
Start of month
Add this month's rows to Rent payments for every active tenant
Send rent reminders a few days before the due date
Review open maintenance requests and schedule vendors
After the due date
Mark payments as Paid, Partial or Late
Send a written late notice to any tenant past the grace period

End of month
File receipts and invoices in the Documents register

content.text: Move-in / move-out checklist
Move-in
Lease signed by all adults and copy stored
Security deposit and first month's rent received
Walk-through completed with dated photos of every room
Keys handed over and recorded; smoke and CO detectors tested
Move-out
Written notice received and logged with date
Final inspection compared against move-in photos
Keys returned and locks changed if needed
Itemized deposit deduction statement sent within the legal deadline
Notes

Keep one slow, unscheduled afternoon every 3 days
Try at least one onsen, one tea ceremony, one market

data.title: Project Brief: Migrating the Team Wiki to PlexiiWrite

content.text: Purpose

This project moves our team wiki from its current home into PlexiiWrite so the team has one place to find, write and maintain shared knowledge. This brief sets out what we want from the move, what is and is not included, how the work will unfold, and what could go wrong. Project owner: [owner name]. Target completion: [target date].
Goals
The move should achieve four things:
Give the team a single, trusted source of documentation, with the old wiki retired once the move is done.
Preserve the content people actually rely on, with links, structure and attachments intact.
Make pages easier to find and easier to keep current, with a clear owner for each section.
Get the whole team working in PlexiiWrite by default, without a long period of split usage.
Scope

In scope are an audit of existing wiki content, a decision on what to migrate, archive or delete, the migration itself, a new top-level structure in PlexiiWrite, access and permission setup, a short guide for the team, and a read-only period for the old wiki before it is shut down.

Out of scope are rewriting content that is merely dated (we will flag it, not fix it during the move), integrations with other tools unless they are needed to keep current workflows running, and any redesign of how the team documents work beyond the new structure and ownership.
Approach and Timeline
The work runs in five phases. Durations and dates are to be set once the owner has reviewed the size of the current wiki.
Audit and cleanup: inventory every page, mark each as migrate, archive or delete, and assign a section owner. Target: [date].
Structure and setup: build the new hierarchy in PlexiiWrite, configure permissions, and agree naming and page conventions. Target: [date].
Pilot: migrate one or two representative sections, check formatting, links and attachments, and collect feedback from a few team members. Target: [date].
Full migration: move the remaining approved content, fix broken links, and have section owners verify their pages. Target: [date].
Cutover and wind-down: announce the switch, set the old wiki to read-only, answer questions, and archive or shut it down after [length of read-only period]. Target: [date].
Risks

Content loss or damage in transfer. Formatting, embedded files, tables and internal links often break in a move. The pilot and owner verification are there to catch this early, and the old wiki stays available until sign-off.
Migrating clutter. Moving everything unchanged carries old problems into the new tool. The audit step, with real delete and archive decisions, is the main defense.
Slow adoption. If people keep editing the old wiki, the two will drift apart. A firm cutover date, a read-only switch and a short how-to guide reduce this.
Permission mistakes. Pages could end up too open or too restricted. Permissions should be reviewed by the owner before the full migration, not after.
Owner availability. Section owners need time to review their content. Their time should be agreed up front rather than assumed.
Next Steps
Confirm the project owner and section owners, agree the target dates above, and begin the content audit.

content.text: Welcome

Welcome to the support team. This guide covers what to expect in your first week, the tools you will use every day, and how we handle escalations. You are not expected to know everything by Friday. The goal of week one is to be comfortable finding answers, confident in the basic workflow, and clear on when to ask for help.
Read the whole guide once at the start, then keep it open. The escalation section in particular is worth returning to during your first few weeks.
Your first week
The week moves from watching, to working alongside someone, to handling tickets yourself with a safety net. Your manager or onboarding buddy, [buddy name], will adjust the pace to how you are doing.
Day one

Today is about access and orientation. You will get your accounts set up, meet the team, and learn how the team is organized. Spend time reading our product documentation and the internal knowledge base as a customer would, so you understand what people see when they come to us. Introduce yourself in the team channel and book a short chat with [manager name].
Days two and three

You will shadow experienced agents on live tickets and, where applicable, calls or chats. Pay attention to how they open a reply, how they confirm they have understood the problem, and how they decide whether to solve something themselves or pass it on. Ask questions as you go. Most agents say this is where they learned the most.
You will also start working through a set of practice tickets in a safe environment, or drafting replies that your buddy reviews before anything is sent.
Days four and five

You will begin answering real tickets, starting with the simpler categories. Your buddy reviews replies before they go out, at first for every ticket and then for a sample. By the end of the week you should have handled a small queue of straightforward tickets and escalated at least one, so you have been through the whole process once.

At the end of the week, sit down with [manager name] for a review. Bring a list of what felt unclear, which product areas you want to learn more about, and anything in this guide that was wrong or missing.
Tools
You will work in a handful of systems every day. Access is requested on day one, so tell your manager right away if anything is missing.

The helpdesk platform, [helpdesk tool], is where tickets arrive, are assigned, and are resolved. Learn how tags, statuses, and macros or saved replies work early, because they affect how our reporting is read.
The internal knowledge base, [knowledge base tool], holds product answers, known issues, and process documents. When you solve something that is not documented, flag it so it can be added.
Team chat, [chat tool], is for quick questions, handoffs, and incident updates. Use the support channel for questions rather than direct messages, so others can learn from the answer.

The admin or back-office tool, [admin tool], lets you look up customer accounts. Only access what you need to resolve the ticket in front of you, and never share account details outside the approved channels.
The engineering issue tracker, [issue tracker], is where bugs are logged and followed. You will mostly read from it at first, then learn how to file well-formed reports.
If your role includes phone or live chat, you will receive separate training on [phone or chat tool].
How we handle tickets

A good reply does four things. It shows the customer we understood their problem, gives them a clear answer or next step, uses plain language rather than internal jargon, and tells them what happens next if the issue is not resolved immediately.

Before replying, read the full ticket history and check whether the customer has contacted us about this before. Nothing frustrates a customer more than repeating themselves. If you are unsure of an answer, do not guess. Check the knowledge base, ask in the support channel, or escalate. A slower correct answer is better than a fast wrong one.
Our target first response time is [first response target], and our target for resolution is [resolution target]. These are goals to work toward, not reasons to rush a careful answer.
Escalations
Escalating is a normal part of the job and never a sign of failure. The mistake is not escalating, or escalating without enough information to act on.
When to escalate
Escalate when any of these apply:
The issue looks like a bug or outage rather than a usage question.
You cannot resolve it with the documentation and tools you have access to.
The customer is asking for something outside your authority, such as a refund above your limit, an exception to policy, or a contract change.
There is a security or privacy concern, including suspected unauthorized access or a request involving personal data.
The customer is at risk of leaving, is threatening legal action, or has raised the issue publicly.
The customer is distressed or the situation is sensitive, and you feel a more experienced person should take over.
If you are unsure whether something qualifies, ask in the support channel. A quick question costs far less than a missed escalation.
Where escalations go
Different problems go to different places. Confirm the current owners with your manager, and keep this list updated.
Technical bugs and outages go to [engineering escalation route].
Billing, refunds, and account disputes go to [billing escalation route].
Security and privacy concerns go to [security contact or route], and should be raised immediately.
Complaints, legal threats, and high-value or at-risk accounts go to [team lead or manager name].
How to write a good escalation
The person receiving your escalation should be able to act without going back to the customer for basics. Include:
A one-line summary of the problem and its impact.
The customer's name, account, and a link to the ticket.
What the customer expected and what actually happened.
Steps to reproduce the problem, if it is technical, along with any error messages, screenshots, or logs.
What you have already tried and ruled out.
How urgent it is and why, including how many customers appear to be affected.
What you have told the customer so far.
After you escalate

You still own the customer relationship. Tell the customer that the issue has been passed to the right team, what to expect, and when you will next update them, then keep that promise even if the update is that there is no news yet. Keep the ticket updated with any developments, and close the loop with the customer when the issue is resolved. If an escalation sits with no response for longer than expected, follow up in the channel or with [team lead or manager name] rather than waiting.
Handling difficult conversations

Customers who contact support are often frustrated before they write a word. Acknowledge the problem first, apologize where we have genuinely fallen short, and focus on what you can do. Do not take anger personally, and do not make promises you cannot keep. If a conversation becomes abusive, you are not required to absorb it. Follow [abusive customer policy] and bring in a team lead.
Who to ask
For day-to-day questions, your onboarding buddy is [buddy name].
For anything about your schedule, performance, or wellbeing, speak to [manager name].
For tool access problems, contact [IT or admin contact].
For product questions you cannot answer, post in the support channel.
End of week one checklist
By the end of your first week, you should be able to say yes to each of these:
I have access to every tool listed in this guide.
I have read the key knowledge base articles for our most common issues.
I have handled real tickets with review from my buddy.
I know when to escalate and where each type of escalation goes.
I have written at least one escalation using the format above.
I have had my end of week conversation with my manager.
If any of these are not true, tell [manager name]. Fixing a gap in week one is much easier than discovering it in week six.

data.title: How to Write a Good Bug Report

slides.title: How to Write a Good Bug Report
slides.notes: Welcome everyone. This session is about a small skill that saves the whole team a lot of time: writing a bug report that someone else can act on without asking you questions.

slides.title: Why the quality of a report matters
bullets: A vague report starts a back-and-forth before any real work begins
Developers can only fix what they can reproduce
A clear report gets triaged faster and assigned with confidence
Good reports protect the reporter's time as well as the developer's
Duplicates and misunderstandings shrink when details are precise
slides.notes: Frame this as a cost question. Every missing detail turns into a round of questions, and each round delays the fix. A few extra minutes from the reporter saves much more time downstream.

slides.title: The anatomy of a strong report
bullets: A short, specific title that names the problem
Steps to reproduce, numbered and in order
Expected result versus actual result
Environment: device, operating system, browser, app version
Evidence such as a screenshot, recording, or log excerpt
Severity and who is affected, as far as you know
slides.notes: Walk through each element in turn. Stress that expected versus actual is the part people skip most, and it is the part that tells the developer what you believe is wrong.

slides.title: Before and after
bullets: Weak title: "Checkout broken"
Stronger title: "Checkout button does nothing after applying a discount code"
Weak steps: "Try to buy something and it fails"
Stronger steps: numbered actions from a known starting point to the failure
Weak result: "It doesn't work"
Stronger result: what you expected, and what you saw instead
slides.notes: Show the contrast out loud. Ask the room which version they would rather receive on a busy day. The point is that specificity is not extra work for its own sake, it is what makes the report usable.

slides.title: Habits that make reports better
bullets: Reproduce the bug at least once more before filing
Search existing reports to avoid duplicates
Report one issue per ticket
Stick to facts and observations, and keep blame out
Note whether it happens every time or only sometimes
Attach evidence at the moment you see the problem
slides.notes: These are quick habits, not a heavy process. Mention that if you cannot reproduce it reliably, say so plainly in the report. That is useful information, not a failure.

slides.title: Your checklist and next step
bullets: Is the title specific?
Can a stranger follow the steps?
Are expected and actual results both stated?
Is the environment listed and evidence attached?
Use this checklist on your next report
slides.notes: Close by encouraging people to run through this list before they hit submit. If your team has a bug template, point them to it here: [link to bug report template].

Refund policy FAQ

Can I get a refund if I change my mind?

Yes. If you ask within 30 days of purchase, we will refund you in full.

What happens after the first 30 days?

Once the 30 days have passed, we do not offer refunds on payments already made. The one exception is annual plans, covered below.

How do refunds work for annual plans?

Annual plans are refunded pro rata. That means you are refunded for the part of your plan term you have not used, rather than for the whole year. For example, if you cancel with a quarter of the term remaining, the refund covers that remaining quarter.

Does the 30-day full refund apply to annual plans too?

Yes. If you cancel an annual plan within 30 days of purchase, you receive a full refund rather than a pro rata one.

How do I request a refund?

Contact us through [support email or contact page] and include the email address on your account. We will confirm your request and let you know when to expect the money, which is [processing time].
